newsitem.title: UK: Lingering rate agony set to dog U.S. bonds.
newsitem.headline: Lingering rate agony set to dog U.S. bonds.

text.p: Interest rate uncertainty will continue to hobble U.S. Treasuries, regardless of the Federal Reserve's action on Tuesday, making a defensive investment strategy prudent, analysts said on Monday.
Investors should stay neutral or short, lie low in one- or two-year notes or look to parts of Europe instead, analysts said. Longer term however, Treasuries were primed to outstrip European debt.
"I would be very defensively in Treasuries," Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London, said. "In terms of risk reward, by far the safest bet...is the very front end of the U.S. market."

Analysts said the chances of a rate rise after the U.S. central bank's Federal Open Market Committee meeting (FOMC) on Tuesday were a toss up. Recent U.S. data, including industrial production and retail sales, have been soft.
Comments from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan have been cryptic, noting both an expected slowdown in demand and the need to take action if the slowdown did not materialise.

June Eurodollar futures were implying three month money at around six percent in three months time while the spread between two-and 30-year yields was at 65 basis points, unchanged since the last rate rise in March.
Before that rise, which took the federal funds target rate to 5.50 percent from 5.25, the market was much more certain of a move and the curve flattened.
"In terms of what is discounted in the market, it's probably 60-40 against a tightening tomorrow," Burke said.
Analysts said a rise would imply the Fed was braced for stronger economic data, although its impact on Treasuries may be ameliorated by a rebound in the dollar.
No rate rise and Treasuries would be put back into suspended animation, waiting for the Fed's next move at the next FOMC meeting in July.
Such uncertainty warrants care, said Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London.
"Near term we would adopt a cautious stance. We don't think there's so much upside if they leave rates unchanged. The best strategy is to be neutral or short," he said.

Ties Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London, expected Treasuries to forge ahead of European debt longer term but required a clear sign U.S. growth was slowing before he would dive in.

"There is a good chance the next big move in Treasuries will be a bull market but we need to see a slow down in the economy and until we do that we will have range trading more than anything else," he said.
He expected the long bond yield to vacillate between 6.75 and 7.25 percent.
Burke at Citibank was not so optimistic on Treasuries.

"The economy is still exceptionally strong. There are no headwinds in terms of what has happened as a result of the last tightening -- the dollar is actually lower, bond yields are lower " he said. "No economy, especially not one as large as the U.S. makes a sudden U-turn."
He favoured one-to-two-year T-notes.
"The high rates on offer with two-years at 6.25 percent compares very favourably with anything you can get in 10-years in Europe," he said.
He added he would make two exceptions -- the front end of the Italian rate curve to take advantage of expected interest rate cuts and British gilts, to ride an expected fall in government borrowing.
